healthcare.summary: Health & medication guide for Croatia. Emergency numbers (112/194/192/193), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, travel insurance, and vaccination recommendations for travelers.

recommended: tick-borne encephalitis (if hiking in inland forested areas)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. Ensure routine vaccinations are current. Croatia has had sporadic tick-borne encephalitis cases in forested inland regions. Standard precautions for outdoor activities apply.

pharmacy.hours: Most pharmacies open Mon-Fri 8am-8pm, Sat 8am-3pm. Some 24/7 pharmacies in Zagreb and major cities. Look for 'Ljekarna' signs. Tourist areas often have pharmacies with extended hours during summer.
pharmacy.tips: Pharmacists in tourist areas often speak English and German. Many common OTC medications are available. EU prescriptions are accepted. The Croatian pharmacy system is well-developed — look for the green cross sign.

water.notes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Croatia. Croatian tap water is tested regularly and meets EU standards. Bottled water is widely available.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Croatia has good food safety standards. Coastal seafood ( Adriatic fish, shellfish) is generally safe at reputable restaurants. Traditional dishes like pašticada, truffles (Istria), and fresh seafood are highlights. Be cautious with unfamiliar wild plants or mushrooms.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required for tourists, but strongly recommended.
travelInsurance.tips: Croatia is affordable for healthcare compared to Western Europe, but travel insurance is still essential for emergencies and medical evacuation. EHIC covers EU citizens for emergency care at public facilities. Summer travelers should note that island hospitals are limited — air evacuation may be needed for serious conditions.

healthcare.qualityNotes: Good quality healthcare, especially in Zagreb, Split, and coastal tourist areas. Major cities have modern hospitals. English is commonly spoken in tourist areas and hospitals. Rural areas may have fewer English-speaking doctors. Pharmacies are widely available.

medications.generalAdvice: Croatia follows EU/Schengen regulations for medication imports since joining the Schengen area in 2023. EU prescriptions are accepted, while non-EU prescriptions may need verification from a local doctor. For controlled substances, carry a Schengen medical certificate. Croatia's HALMED (Agency for Medicinal Products) oversees pharmaceutical regulation.

controlledSubstances.note: Cannabis is illegal for recreational use in Croatia. Medical cannabis is limited to specific conditions with Croatian prescription only. CBD products with 0% THC are legal. Do not bring any THC-containing products.
Controlled under Croatian narcotics law. Requires Schengen certificate or doctor's letter. Carry only personal-use quantities in original packaging.
Controlled substances. Requires documentation and Schengen certificate. Contact Croatian health authorities or your embassy if you need to bring ADHD medications.
Controlled. EU regulations apply. Carry Schengen certificate, doctor's letter, and original prescription. Customs may inspect quantities.
Croatia has comprehensive legislation banning new psychoactive substances. Possession and import are criminal offenses.

connectivity.simOptions: A1, T-Mobile, or Telemach at airports. EU roaming works since 2023.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Good WiFi at cafes, hotels, restaurants along coast.
connectivity.bestOption: EU SIM with roaming. Otherwise A1 prepaid at airport.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants appreciated. Round up for taxis.
cultural.dressCode: Casual on coast. Cover shoulders/knees in churches. Comfortable shoes in Old Towns.
cultural.greetings: Handshake formal. Kiss on both cheeks between friends. 'Bok' is casual hello.
taboos: Being loud in Old Towns at night
Not trying local wine when offered

safety.lgbtSafety: Croatia has made progress on LGBTQ+ rights as an EU member, with life partnerships legally recognized. Zagreb Pride is well-established. However, conservative attitudes persist, especially outside Zagreb and the coast — public displays of affection between same-sex couples may attract stares in smaller towns.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Croatia is very safe for solo female travelers. The Dalmatian coast, Zagreb, and islands are well-traveled and welcoming. Standard precautions apply at night in cities — stick to well-lit areas and use reputable transport.
safety.notes: Croatia is one of the safest countries in Southern Europe for tourists. Violent crime is very rare. Petty theft can occur in crowded tourist areas along the coast during peak summer season. Landmine remnants from the 1990s war exist in some rural and border areas — stay on marked paths in these regions.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free (Schengen, joined 2023). UK, EU, Australia, Canada also visa-free.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: May-June and September (warm, fewer crowds). July-August peak in Dubrovnik.

immediate: Evacuate damaged buildings immediately after shaking stops
Avoid tall buildings, bridges, and coastal areas after major quake

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 192)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (192) and ambulance (194) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
